title: Into the pit (Genesis 37:12–36)
hookLine: the brothers sell Joseph for twenty pieces of silver

lines: GO AND SEE IF YOUR BROTHERS ARE WELL.
THE COAT, SEEN FROM FAR OFF.
cards: Jacob sends Joseph on an errand: go and see if your brothers are well, out with the flocks, and bring me word. It's a long walk from home. Joseph gets lost in the fields, and a stranger has to point him the right way.

Then there he is on the last ridge, the boy in the coat, visible from far off. His brothers see him before he can see their faces. And one of them says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold the dreamer cometh."
By the time he reaches them, they've already decided.

teach.h: LET'S KILL HIM, AND SEE HIS DREAMS.
teach.b: First, the plot. Come, the brothers say, let's kill him, throw him into a pit, say a wild beast ate him, and see what becomes of his dreams. Reuben, the eldest, pushes back: don't kill him, just throw him in the pit.
He planned, Genesis says, to come back later and rescue him. Then the pit. They strip off the coat, that coat, and throw him into an old cistern.
It's empty, the text says. No water in it. And then, without a word of comment from Genesis, they sit down to eat bread.
Then the sale. A caravan comes by, carrying spices down to Egypt. Judah speaks up: what profit is there in killing our brother?
Let's sell him; he's our own flesh.
They pull him out of the pit and, in the Douay-Rheims, "sold him to the Ismaelites, for twenty pieces of silver." Reuben comes back, finds the pit empty, and tears his clothes. Last, the lie.
The brothers kill a young goat, dip the coat in its blood, and send it to their father: do you know this coat?

Jacob, who once wore goatskins to deceive his own blind father, is now deceived by goat's blood on his son's coat. He tears his garments and refuses to be comforted. I will go down to my son mourning, he says.
Church Fathers such as Ambrose read Joseph as a figure of Christ: the beloved son, sent by his father to his brothers, rejected by his own, sold for silver, and carried down into Egypt.

how: The Church keeps February 8, the feast of Saint Josephine Bakhita, a Sudanese woman sold into slavery as a child who became a Canossian sister, as a world day of prayer against human trafficking.

practice: Joseph's story is ancient, but it isn't over: somewhere today, people are bought and sold, forced to work and kept from home, sometimes by people who should have protected them.
Picture one person far from home who can't leave, and stay with them. If you pray, ask for their freedom and for someone to find them; if you don't, simply hold them in your mind.
